rationale: A wins because it keeps the angles structurally different and mostly stays honest about what must be proven before anyone pitches. Its best move is “Khan Academy is putting AI tutors in front of 1 million students. The study saying it works hasn't been peer-reviewed,” which gives a reporter tension, evidence, and a real editor-safe question. B has good bones, but “As Khanmigo scales, Khan Academy answers the independent-thinking critics directly” invents a response the facts do not give you. That is how a pitch walks itself into a wall.
gaps_in_A: “districts are signing on to expand to 1 million students based on a study” overstates causality. The update says the rollout and results are happening together; it does not say districts expanded because of the study.

“a body of research on productive failure and desirable difficulty argues” imports outside pedagogy context as if it is already established in the supplied facts. Fine as proof to seek; not fine as a stated premise.
“While VC-backed EdTech companies charge districts” is an unsourced market contrast. Useful if documented, but the update only says Khan is nonprofit, free to teachers, and donor-funded.
gaps_in_B: “Khan Academy answers the independent-thinking critics directly” is invented. The update says some educators question the effect on independent thinking; it does not say Khan has answered them.
“30 districts signing on simultaneously” and “through 30 districts at once” overclaim the rollout mechanics. The facts say 30 more districts, not a synchronized adoption event.
“public-school students” is a small but unnecessary embellishment. The facts say US school districts; do not add category precision you were not given.
B leaves the teacher lesson-planning fact on the floor. “Khanmigo gives teachers lesson-planning help” could support a sharper teacher-workload angle than the padded adoption-trend slot.
